themes.name: Greetings & Courtesy
themes.intro: Kumusta! I'm Lumpy, your friendly lumpia. Let's learn how Filipinos say hello, please, and thank you — tara, let's go!

items.n: Borrowed from the Spanish 'cómo está', this is the universal, friendly greeting for asking how someone is doing or simply saying hello.
A polite morning greeting made by combining 'maganda' (beautiful/good) with 'umaga' (morning).
Used to greet people in the afternoon. 'Hapon' translates to afternoon in Tagalog.
Standard evening greeting used from sundown onwards. 'Gabi' means night.
Used to say goodbye when parting ways. It carries a sense of finality for the day or interaction.
The standard way to express gratitude. You can add 'po' at the end for extra politeness.
Literally translates to 'there is nothing', used as the standard polite response to 'Salamat'.
An apology derived from Spanish 'paciencia'. Used to ask for patience or forgiveness for a mistake.
Added to requests to make them polite, roughly equivalent to 'please' in English.
The direct Tagalog word for 'yes'.
The standard word for 'no' or negation in Tagalog statements.
A warm parting wish meaning 'take care', often said to someone leaving.

sentences.speaker: lumpy
sentences.n: The subject pronoun 'ka' (you) directly follows the greeting 'kumusta'. This is a very common sentence structure in Tagalog conversational greetings.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: The preposition 'sa' links the expression of thanks ('salamat') to the object being thanked for ('tulong' or help).

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: A concise directive where the verb or state 'ingat' precedes the second-person pronoun 'ka'.

themes.name: People & Pronouns
themes.intro: Hi! I'm Jetjet! Let's learn who everybody is — ako, ikaw, siya — so you can talk about the whole family. Game?

items.n: Ako means I or me. It is a personal pronoun that usually comes before the word it relates to.
Ikaw means you. Note that ikaw is used at the beginning of a sentence, while 'ka' is used after verbs or adjectives.
Siya means he or she. Tagalog pronouns are gender-neutral, so siya applies equally to males and females.
Kami means we, but it is exclusive—it means me and others, but NOT you (the person being spoken to).
Tayo means we, and it is inclusive—it includes both the speaker and you (the listener).
Kayo means you all, used when addressing a group of two or more people respectfully or collectively.
Sila means they. It refers to a group of people other than the speaker and the listener.
Lalaki means man or male. It can also function as an adjective to describe male animals or items.
Babae means woman or female. It is commonly used for both people and female animals.
Bata means child or kid. It can also describe someone who is young in age.
Kaibigan means friend. You can add 'ko' at the end to say 'my friend'.
Tao means person or human. It can also refer to people in general when used in conversation.

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: This sentence uses the inverted word order with the linker 'ay'. The subject 'Ako' comes first, followed by 'ay', and then the noun complement 'lalaki'.

sentences.e: He or she is my friend.
sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This sentence connects the pronoun 'siya' to the noun phrase 'kaibigan ko' using the formal linker 'ay'.

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: This sentence uses the subject pronoun 'kami' followed by the linker 'ay' and the adjective 'masaya' to describe the group's state.

themes.name: Introductions
themes.intro: Time to introduce yourself! I'm Lumpy, and by the end of this one you'll be able to say who you are and where you're from. Halika!

items.n: Pangalan means name. When asking someone's name, you use 'Anong pangalan mo?' which literally translates to 'What your name?'.
This phrase introduces yourself by saying 'I am Ana'. The word 'si' acts as a personal marker before a proper name.
This is the standard way to ask 'What is your name?'. 'Anong' is a contraction of 'Ano ang' meaning 'What is the'.
'Taga-saan' asks about a person's origin or hometown, translating to 'From where'.
Use 'Taga-' followed by a place name to state where you are from. 'Ako' means 'I'.
Pilipino refers to a person of Philippine nationality or the Filipino language itself.
Ingles is the Tagalog word for the English language, borrowed from Spanish origins.
Tagalog is one of the major languages spoken in the Philippines and serves as the basis for the national language, Filipino.
This verb form indicates that someone is currently studying or a student.
Guro is the Tagalog word for teacher. You can use it to address or describe educators.
Maganda means beautiful or pretty. It can describe people, places, or things.
Masaya means happy or joyful. It is commonly used to describe feelings or cheerful occasions.

sentences.speaker: lumpy
sentences.n: Tagalog sentences often use a predicate-first structure. Here, the pronoun 'Ako' comes first, followed by the marker 'si' and the proper name.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This question puts the interrogative predicate first, followed by the noun and the possessive pronoun 'mo' meaning 'your'.

sentences.speaker: lumpy
sentences.n: The origin indicator 'Taga-Australia' starts the sentence, establishing context before the subject pronoun 'ako' at the end.

themes.name: Family
themes.intro: Halika, apo! Lola Joli here — family is everything in the Philippines, so let's learn the words for the people you love most.

items.n: Pamilya refers to your family. It is borrowed from the Spanish 'familia'.
Nanay is a warm, affectionate term for mother. It is very commonly used in everyday Filipino homes.
Tatay is the standard affectionate word for father. You can also hear 'Itay' as a variation.
Kapatid means sibling, covering both brothers and sisters. It literally translates to sharing the same womb.
Kuya is used to address or refer to an older brother. It is also respectfully used for older male cousins or close family friends.
Ate refers to an older sister. Like 'kuya', it is often used respectfully for older female relatives or acquaintances.
Lolo is the Tagalog word for grandfather. You can attach it to a name, like Lolo Juan.
Lola means grandmother. It is often used with great affection for any elderly woman.
Anak means child or offspring. Parents frequently use it as a term of endearment for their children regardless of age.
Asawa means spouse, husband, or wife. It is a gender-neutral term in Tagalog.
Pamilya ko means 'my family'. The word 'ko' functions as the possessive pronoun 'my' and comes after the noun.
Mabait means kind, good-natured, or well-behaved. It is frequently used to describe family members and friends.

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: This sentence uses a predicate-first structure. 'Malaki' (big) comes first, followed by the marker 'ang' and the subject 'pamilya ko'.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This follows the standard Tagalog sentence structure where the descriptive adjective comes first as the predicate, followed by the subject.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: Here, 'Mahal' (love) is the predicate, 'ko' indicates the doer (I), and 'ang pamilya ko' is the direct object being loved.

sentences.e: He or she is my child.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal

themes.name: Food Basics
themes.intro: Lola Joli's kitchen is open! Rice, chicken, fish — let's learn the words, and then we'll eat. Gutom ka na ba?

items.n: Pagkain is the general Tagalog word for food. It comes from the root word kain, which means to eat.
Kanin specifically refers to cooked rice, which is a staple of almost every Filipino meal. Uncooked rice in the sack or field is called bigas.
Tinapay is the word for bread. It is commonly eaten during breakfast or as an afternoon snack called merienda.
Itlog means egg. It is a breakfast favorite in the Philippines, often served with garlic rice and meat.
Karne is a loanword from the Spanish word carne, meaning meat. It usually refers to beef, pork, or other livestock.
Manok means chicken. Chicken is one of the most popular meats in Filipino cuisine and is used in many dishes like adobo and tinola.
Baboy means pig or pork. Pork is widely consumed in the Philippines and is the star of famous dishes like lechon.
Isda means fish. Being an archipelago, the Philippines has an abundance of fresh seafood and fish is a dietary staple.
Gulay means vegetables. Filipinos incorporate various local greens and vegetables into stews, soups, and side dishes.
Prutas is a loanword from the Spanish frutas, meaning fruit. Tropical fruits like mangoes and bananas are abundant.
Masarap means delicious or tasty. You will use this word often to compliment someone's cooking.
In Tagalog, adjectives like 'gutom' (hungry) act as the predicate and come first, followed by the pronoun 'ako' (I).

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This simple sentence places the descriptive state first, followed immediately by the subject pronoun indicating who is feeling that way.

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: The verb 'kumakain' (is eating) begins the sentence in the ongoing aspect. The word 'ng' acts as a grammatical marker linking the verb to its direct object 'kanin'.

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: This equational sentence begins with the adjective 'masarap' (delicious). The article 'ang' marks 'pagkain' (food) as the subject of the sentence.

sentences.e: Ate Crystal is eating a mango.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal

sentences.t: Kumakain kami ng isda at gulay.
sentences.e: We are eating fish and vegetables.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

themes.name: Drinks & Fruit
themes.intro: Tita Baby here — let's keep it simple: water, coffee, and the sweetest mangoes you'll ever taste. Kape tayo?

items.n: Tubig is the Tagalog word for water. You will use this constantly throughout the day in the tropical heat.
Kape means coffee. Filipinos love their morning coffee, often pairing it with pan de sal bread.
Tsaa refers to tea. It is borrowed from Chinese origins, specifically through the Hokkien tea trade.
Gatas translates to milk. It is commonly used in breakfast meals or added to local coffee.
Juice is directly adopted from English. It is a very common term for any fruit juice.
Saging means banana. The Philippines grows many delicious varieties, including saba and lakatan.
Mangga is the word for mango. The Philippine mango is world-famous for being exceptionally sweet.
Mansanas means apple. It comes from the Spanish word 'manzana' introduced during colonial times.
Pinya translates to pineapple. The country is a major exporter of this sweet and tangy tropical fruit.
Ubas means grapes. They are a popular fruit often bought at local markets and supermarkets.
Matamis describes something that is sweet in taste, like ripe mangoes or desserts.
Uhaw ako translates to I am thirsty. Use this helpful phrase whenever you need a cold drink.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This simple sentence places the predicate adjective 'uhaw' first, followed by the pronoun 'ako' meaning I.

sentences.speaker: ate-crystal
sentences.n: The verb 'umiinom' (drinking) starts the sentence in an active voice. The word 'ng' marks the direct object 'tubig'.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: This structure uses the possessive pronoun 'ko' with 'gusto' to express personal preference, followed by 'ng' for the object.

themes.name: Numbers 1-12
themes.intro: Counting is easy — and I need it for my Beyblade battles! Isa, dalawa, tatlo... let's count together!

items.n: Means one. Used both for counting objects and in basic arithmetic.
Means two. Often used with 'ang' to state possession or quantities of family and items.
Means three. Pronounced with equal stress on syllables.
Means four. A straightforward number word used in daily counting.
Means five. Also shares its spelling with the capital city of Peru, but here it is the number five.
Means six. Notice the short vowel sound in everyday conversation.
Means seven. Commonly used when telling time or counting objects.
Means eight. Used in counting money, time, and quantities.
Means nine. Be careful with pronunciation to distinguish it from similar sounds.
Means ten. Reaching sampu completes the basic single digits.
Means eleven. Formed by combining 'labing-' with 'isa' to indicate numbers past ten.
Means twelve. Combines the prefix for tens with 'dalawa'.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: The focus is on the possessor ('ko' meaning my). 'Dalawa' comes first to state the quantity, followed by 'ang' and the noun phrase 'kapatid ko'.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: 'Mga' pluralizes 'bata' (child), making it 'children'. The number 'sampu' starts the sentence to indicate the total count.

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: The particle 'na' translates roughly to 'already'. The phrase literally means 'Already seven is the time', which is the standard way to state the hour.

sentences.t: Apat na pusa ang nakikita ko.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong

sentences.e: There are five birds on the tree.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal

sentences.t: Anim na saging ang binili ko.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

themes.name: Time & Days
themes.intro: Tita Baby here — mornings, nights, today, tomorrow. If you know the time, you know when dinner's ready. Let's go.

items.n: Oras means time or hour. It comes from the Spanish 'horas'.
Ngayon means now or today. It is used very frequently in daily conversation.
Mamaya means later (referring to the future, usually later today).
Kanina means earlier today or a little while ago. It refers to the past within the same day.
Kahapon means yesterday. It places an action on the day before today.
Araw means both 'day' and 'sun'. Context will tell you whether the speaker means the twenty-four-hour period or the bright star in the sky.
Bukas means tomorrow. Note that spelled differently with a different accent, 'bukas' can also mean open.
Umaga means morning. People often greet each other with 'Magandang umaga' (Good morning).
Tanghali refers to noon or midday, right around lunchtime.
Hapon means afternoon. Do not confuse it with the nationality 'Hapon' (Japanese), which is spelled the same way.
Gabi means night or evening. It is used when greeting someone in the evening ('Magandang gabi').
Linggo means week. It also refers to the day Sunday.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: The pronoun 'ako' becomes 'akong' using the linker '-ng' because it follows the adverb 'maaga'. Word order puts the descriptor first.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: The word 'ay' acts as a polite inversion marker connecting the topic 'bukas' to the predicate 'may pasok'.

sentences.speaker: ate-crystal
sentences.n: The adjective 'masaya' comes first, followed by the subject 'ang araw' and the time marker 'ngayon'.

sentences.t: Mainit ang ulo ko ngayong umaga.
sentences.e: I am in a bad mood this morning.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal

themes.name: Places in Town
themes.intro: Tito Bong here! I'll show you around town — the palengke, the church, the bank. Sunod ka lang sa akin!

items.n: Bahay means house or home. It is often combined with other words to form compound locations like 'bahay-kalakal' (business house).
Eskwelahan comes from the Spanish 'escuela' adapted into Tagalog. It refers to a school or educational institution.
Ospital is a direct loanword from the Spanish 'hospital'. You will also hear the Tagalog-derived word 'paggagamutan'.
Botika means pharmacy or drugstore, derived from the Spanish 'botica'. It is where people buy medicines and health supplies.
Simbahan refers to a church. The root word 'simba' means to attend church services.
Tindahan is a small store or shop, derived from the root 'tinda' meaning to sell. It is a very common everyday vocabulary word.
Palengke means market or wet market, borrowed from the Spanish 'palenque'. It is where locals buy fresh meat, fish, and vegetables.
Bangko means bank, borrowed from Spanish. Note that 'bangko' with a slightly different intonation can also mean bench or stool.
Hotel refers to a hotel for lodging. It is pronounced similarly to the English word and is widely understood.
Tanggapan means office or reception area, coming from the root 'tanggap' which means to accept or receive.
Kalsada means street or road, coming from the Spanish 'calzada'. It is used for paved roads in towns and cities.
Banyo means bathroom or restroom, adapted from the Spanish 'baño'. It is an essential term when navigating public places.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: This sentence uses the location marker 'nasa' followed by the place 'bahay', and ends with the pronoun 'ako' (I).

sentences.e: I am going to the market.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: The verb 'pupunta' is in the future tense, indicating an action that will happen. The preposition 'sa' introduces the destination 'palengke'.

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: This is an equational sentence starting with the adjective 'malapit' (nearby), followed by the topic marker 'ang' and the subject 'tindahan'.

sentences.e: Grandma Joli is at the hospital.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli

sentences.e: We are going to the school.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

sentences.e: Auntie Baby is at the pharmacy.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

themes.name: Directions
themes.intro: Left, right, straight ahead — Tito Bong never gets lost. Well, almost never. Let's learn to find your way!

items.n: Saan is the primary question word for asking about location. When asking where something is located, it is often combined with the particle 'ang'.
Kaliwa means left. It is commonly used with directional verbs like 'lumiko' to give driving or walking instructions.
Kanan means right. Like 'kaliwa', it pairs frequently with directional verbs and prepositions.
Deretso means straight ahead. When giving directions, saying 'deretso lang' tells someone to keep going without turning.
Malapit means near or close. It can describe physical distance or a place that is close by.
Malayo means far. It is the opposite of malapit and indicates a significant distance.
Dito means here. It points to a location close to the speaker.
Doon means there. It points to a location away from both the speaker and the listener.
Harap means front. It is often used in locational phrases like 'sa harap ng' to mean in front of.
Likod means back or behind. It is used to specify the rear side of an object or building.
Taas means up, high, or above. It can refer to upper floors in a building or an upward direction.
Baba means down or below. It can mean going downstairs or getting off a vehicle.

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: This sentence starts with the imperative verb 'lumiko' (turn), followed by the actor pronoun 'ka' (you), and the directional marker 'sa' pointing to 'kaliwa'.

sentences.speaker: lumpy
sentences.n: This is a concise, everyday command using 'deretso' (straight) paired with the limiter 'lang' (just/only), commonly used by commuters and drivers.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This existential-locational question uses 'nasaan' to ask for the exact location of the noun 'ang banyo'.

sentences.e: The car is at the back.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal

themes.name: Transport
themes.intro: Bus, train, jeepney — Tito Bong has ridden them all! Let's learn how to get around the Philippines.

items.n: Sasakyan generally means vehicle or transport, and can also be used as a verb meaning to ride or board something.
Borrowed from English, bus refers to the large public motor vehicle used widely for commuting in the Philippines.
Tren comes from Spanish and refers to a train, commonly used when discussing rail transit.
Derived from Spanish aeroplano, this word means airplane and is used for air travel.
Bangka is the traditional Filipino word for a boat or canoe, often seen traversing coastal waters.
The iconic jeepney is the most popular indigenous mode of shared public transport in the Philippines, decorated colorfully.
Taksi is a phonetic Tagalog spelling of the English word taxi, used for metered cabs.
Drayber is the Tagalog phonetic adaptation of the English word driver, specifically someone operating a vehicle.
Borrowed from Spanish pasajero, pasahero refers to a passenger riding in any vehicle.
Istasyon comes from the Spanish estación, meaning a station for trains or other transport hubs.
Tiket is the local spelling adaptation of the English word ticket, required for boarding certain transport.
Biyahe comes from Spanish viaje, meaning a trip, journey, or travel.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This sentence uses actor-focus verb syntax where 'sasakyan' acts as the future tense verb 'will take', followed by the pronoun 'ko' (by me) and the nominative marker 'ang' introducing the subject 'bus'.

sentences.e: The train is at the station.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: This sentence begins with the locative prefix 'nasa' (located at) attached to the place 'istasyon', followed by the subject 'ang tren'.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: This is an equational descriptive sentence starting with the adjective 'mahal' (expensive), followed by the subject marker 'ang' and 'tiket'.

sentences.e: How much is the boat ticket?
sentences.speaker: lola-joli

themes.name: Travel & Hotels
themes.intro: Pack your bags! Passport, luggage, room key — Tito Bong's guide to travelling like a pro.

items.n: Bakasyon refers to a vacation or holiday, often used when travelling or taking a break from work or school.
Pasaporte is a direct loanword from the Spanish pasaporte, meaning passport.
Maleta means luggage or suitcase. It is commonly used when packing for a trip.
Kuwarto means room, derived from the Spanish cuarto. It refers to a bedroom or hotel room.
Susi means key. You will need this to unlock your hotel kuwarto.
Paliparan means airport. It comes from the root word lipar, related to flying.
Daungan means port or dock where ships and boats arrive.
Mapa means map. It is essential for navigating a new place during your travels.
Kamera means camera. Use this to take larawan during your trip.
Larawan means photo or picture.
Sandali means a moment or a short while. Often used to ask someone to wait.
Hinto means a stop or halt, often used in transit or directions.

sentences.e: I am going to the airport.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal
sentences.n: This sentence uses the future tense verb 'pupunta' (will go) first, followed by the subject 'ako' (I) and the location 'sa paliparan' (to the airport).

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: 'Nasaan' asks for the location of something. The phrase 'ng kuwarto' shows possession, indicating it is the key belonging to the room.

sentences.speaker: lumpy
sentences.n: This expresses need using 'kailangan' followed by 'ko' (my/by me) and 'ng mapa' (a map), forming a standard possession and necessity structure.

sentences.t: Teka lang, kunin ko ang kamera.
sentences.e: Wait a moment, I will get the camera.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong

sentences.t: May hinto ba ang bus dito?
sentences.e: Does the bus have a stop here?
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

sentences.e: The photo at the port is beautiful.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal

sentences.t: Handa na ba ang pasaporte mo?
sentences.speaker: jetjet

themes.name: Shopping
themes.intro: Lola Joli knows the palengke like the back of her hand — and she never pays full price! Let's learn to shop, apo.

items.n: Bumili is the past/completed tense of the verb 'to buy'. It uses the um- infix to indicate that the action has already been performed.
Magkano is the standard interrogative word used specifically to ask for the price of goods or services when shopping.
Mura describes something that is inexpensive or low in cost. It can apply to items, food, or general services.
Mahal has a dual meaning in Tagalog: it can mean expensive when discussing prices, or dear and beloved when describing people.
Sukli refers to the physical coins or paper bills returned to a buyer as change after a cash transaction.
Tindera refers specifically to a female vendor or shopkeeper. The male equivalent is usually tindero.
Damit is a general term for clothing, garments, or apparel worn on the body.
Sapatos is a borrowed word from Spanish (zapatos) referring to footwear or shoes.
Bag is commonly used in modern conversational Tagalog to refer to a handbag, backpack, or purse, borrowed from English.
Tawad means asking for a discount or bargaining on a price, which is a common practice in local markets.
Bayad is the noun for payment or fare given in exchange for goods or services.
Resibo is a Spanish-derived term (recibo) used to mean a receipt or proof of purchase.

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: This question places the interrogative word 'magkano' first, followed by the demonstrative pronoun 'ito' (this) without needing a linker.

sentences.speaker: ate-crystal
sentences.n: The sentence begins with the completed verb 'bumili', followed by the actor pronoun 'ako' and the object marker 'ng' introducing 'sapatos'.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: This descriptive sentence places the adjective 'mahal' first, followed by the subject marker 'ang' and the noun 'damit'.

sentences.e: Can I ask for a discount?
sentences.speaker: lumpy

sentences.t: Gusto ko ang bag na ito.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

sentences.e: Here is the payment and receipt.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

themes.name: Clothes
themes.intro: New shoes, new shirt, new hat — Ate Crystal here! Let's talk clothes, on and off the court.

items.n: Damit is a general term for clothes or clothing in Tagalog. It can refer to any type of garment.
Kamiseta is a loanword from Spanish (camiseta) meaning a T-shirt or jersey. It is commonly used in daily conversation.
Pantalon means pants or trousers, adapted from the Spanish word pantalón. It is used for both casual and formal pants.
Sapatos refers to shoes and comes from the Spanish zapatos. It covers all kinds of footwear like sneakers and dress shoes.
Sombrero is the Tagalog word for a hat, borrowed from Spanish. It can refer to caps, sun hats, or other headwear.
Medyas means socks, coming from the Spanish medias. It is used for any kind of foot coverings worn inside shoes.
Dyaket is the Tagalog phonetic spelling for jacket, borrowed from English. It is handy for cooler weather or rain.
Palda means skirt, originating from the Spanish falda. It is a common clothing term used across the Philippines.
Baro is a traditional Tagalog word for shirt or dress. It is often part of compound words like barong Tagalog.
Sinturon means belt, adapted from the Spanish cinturón. It is the accessory used to hold up pants.
Bago means new. It can also mean 'before' depending on the sentence structure, but here it describes a new item.
Luma means old, specifically referring to things that are used, worn out, or aged, rather than elderly people.

sentences.speaker: ate-crystal
sentences.n: This sentence uses inverted order where the predicate 'Bago' comes first, followed by the subject 'ang sapatos ko' (my shoes).

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: The phrase 'Suot ko' means 'worn by me' or 'I am wearing', putting the focus on the state of wearing the clothing item.

sentences.t: Gusto ko ang bago kong sombrero.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: The linker '-ng' connects the adjective 'bago' to the noun modifier 'kong', showing that the newness belongs to the hat.

sentences.t: Gusto ko ang baro na ito.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli

themes.name: At Home
themes.intro: Welcome to Lola Joli's house, apo! Kitchen, bedroom, window, door — let's learn your way around a Filipino home.

items.n: Kuwarto refers to a room, most commonly a bedroom in a home. It is a loanword derived from Spanish.
Hapag usually refers to a table, often specifically a dining table or 'hapag-kainan'.
Upuan is any chair or seat. It comes from the root word 'upo', meaning to sit.
Kama is the bed where you sleep or rest. It is a very common household term.
Bintana means window and is another loanword of Spanish origin widely used in everyday Tagalog.
Pinto is a door. You can open (bukas) or close (sarado) it.
Bubong refers to the roof of a house or building, protecting people from rain and sun.
Kusina is the kitchen where meals are prepared. It is adapted from the Spanish 'cocina'.
Lababo is the sink, used for washing hands, dishes, or food items in the kitchen or bathroom.
Ilaw means light or lamp. It illuminates dark rooms at night.
Kandado means lock, typically a padlock used to secure doors or gates.
Gripo is the faucet or tap where running water comes out.

sentences.e: My mother is in the kitchen.
sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This sentence uses the locative marker 'nasa' to indicate that the mother is located inside the kitchen. The subject 'ang nanay ko' follows the location.

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: This is a descriptive sentence placing the adjective 'sarado' first, followed by the subject 'ang pinto' with the article 'ang'.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: This sentence follows a predicate-subject structure where the state 'bukas' comes first, describing the subject 'ang bintana'.

sentences.e: Grandma Joli is in the room.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli

sentences.e: The sink in the kitchen is clean.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal

sentences.e: The light at the table is bright.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong

themes.name: Daily Routine
themes.intro: Tita Baby runs a tight ship — wake up, shower, breakfast, work. Learn the routine and your day runs itself!

items.n: Gising means awake. It is often used as an adjective or an exclamation to tell someone to wake up.
Tulog means sleep or asleep. You can use it to describe someone who is currently resting or sleeping soundly.
Maligo is an active verb meaning to take a bath or shower. In tropical Philippines, bathing often happens multiple times a day!
Bumihis means to get dressed. It is an action word focusing on putting on your clothes for the day.
Kain is the root word for eating. Filipinos often greet each other with 'Kain na!' which means 'Let's eat!'
Inom is the base word for drinking. It refers to consuming any liquid, from water to coffee.
Trabaho means work or job. It is a loanword derived from Spanish, commonly used in everyday conversations.
Eskwela means school. It is another Spanish-derived word, alongside the native Tagalog equivalent 'paaralan'.
Pahinga means rest or taking a break. It is essential for recharging during a busy daily routine.
Laba refers to doing the laundry. It specifically describes washing clothes, often done by hand or in a machine.
Luto means to cook or cooked. It describes the preparation of meals, which is a big part of daily life.
Linis means to clean. It is used when doing chores around the house or tidying up a space.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: This sentence uses the actor-focus verb 'gumigising' (waking up) in the present tense. 'Ako' means 'I', and 'nang maaga' means 'early'.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: The verb 'kumakain' is in the progressive aspect, indicating an ongoing action. 'Ng' marks the object 'almusal' (breakfast).

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: 'Pumapasok' means going in or entering. The preposition 'sa' indicates direction toward 'trabaho' (work).

sentences.t: Naliligo ako sa bago kong banyo.
sentences.e: I am showering in my new bathroom.
sentences.speaker: lumpy

sentences.t: Umiinom ako ng mainit na kape.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong

sentences.t: Nagluluto si nanay ng masarap na pagkain.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

sentences.e: I am studying at school today.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

sentences.e: I am resting in the room for a moment.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli

themes.name: Weather
themes.intro: A beekeeper always watches the sky! Hot, rainy, sunny — Lola Joli will teach you to talk about the weather like a Filipino.

items.n: Panahon means both 'weather' and 'season' or 'era' in Tagalog. It is a versatile word used to talk about atmospheric conditions or general times.
Mainit describes something that is hot in temperature, such as weather, water, or food. It can also describe a person's hot temper.
Malamig is used for cold weather, cold objects, or chilly temperatures. It is the exact opposite of mainit.
Maaraw is an adjective formed by adding the prefix ma- to araw. It literally means 'having sun' or sunny.
Maulan means rainy, derived from the root word ulan with the prefix ma-. You will hear this frequently during the monsoon season.
Ulan refers to rain itself as a noun. When it is falling, you often use the verb form umuulan.
Araw means both 'sun' and 'day'. Context usually makes it clear whether you are talking about the celestial body or a 24-hour period.
Buwan means 'moon' and also 'month'. It is identical in form for both celestial and calendar meanings.
Hangin means wind, air, or breeze. It is commonly used when talking about a draft or a windy day.
Bagyo means storm or typhoon. The Philippines experiences many bagyo each year, making this a very common weather term.
Kulog refers to the sound of thunder. It often pairs with kidlat during stormy weather.
Kidlat means lightning. You will often see it mentioned right alongside kulog when describing a thunderstorm.

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: This sentence uses the basic equational or descriptive order where the adjective 'mainit' comes first, followed by the topic marker 'ang' and the subject.

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: Umuulan is the present tense verb for raining. 'Sa labas' acts as a locational phrase meaning 'outside'.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: A concise descriptive sentence stating that it is sunny today. 'Ngayon' places the state in the present time.

sentences.e: There is an incoming storm tomorrow.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong

sentences.e: Did you all hear any thunder?
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

sentences.e: The lightning and thunder are scary.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

themes.name: Nature
themes.intro: Sea, mountain, river, trees — Jetjet loves the outdoors! Let's learn the words for the world around us.

items.n: Dagat means sea or ocean. It is often used when talking about going to the beach or coastal areas.
Bundok means mountain. You will use this word when talking about hiking or viewing nature landscapes.
Ilog means river. It refers to a natural flowing body of water, often found near rural areas or forests.
Lawa means lake. It describes an inland body of standing water, distinct from the sea.
Kagubatan means forest. It is a derivative of 'gubat', meaning woods or jungle, with the prefix and suffix indicating a large area.
Bulaklak means flower. It is also commonly used to refer to blossoms on plants and trees.
Puno means tree. Note that 'puno' can also mean full in a completely different context depending on sentence structure.
Ibon means bird. You will often hear this when talking about animals that fly.
Hayop means animal. It serves as a general term for all kinds of creatures.
Langit means sky or heaven. It is used to describe the atmosphere above or the celestial realm.
Bituin means star. In poetic or musical contexts, you might also hear the synonym 'tala'.
Buhangin means sand. It is commonly used when describing beaches or deserts.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This sentence uses the basic actor-predicate or descriptive order where the adjective 'malaki' comes first, followed by the topic marker 'ang' and the noun.

sentences.e: The boat is on the sea.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: The phrase 'nasa' indicates location. Here, it places the subject ('ang bangka') at a specific location ('dagat').

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: This is a descriptive sentence starting with the adjective 'maganda', followed by the subject 'ang bulaklak' (the flower).

sentences.e: The water in the river is cold.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong

sentences.e: The bird sang on the tree.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

sentences.e: The sand on the shore is hot.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

themes.name: Feelings
themes.intro: Happy, tired, nervous before a big match — Ate Crystal feels it all! Let's learn to say how you feel.

items.n: Masaya means happy. It is commonly used to describe both a person's current emotional state and the general mood of a gathering or event.
Malungkot means sad. It comes from the root word 'lungkot', meaning sadness, with the prefix 'ma-' indicating the presence of that feeling.
Galit means angry. When you want to say you are angry at someone, you typically combine it with the preposition 'sa'.
Takot means afraid or scared. It can be used alone to express fear or paired with 'sa' to specify what someone is afraid of.
Pagod means tired. This is frequently used after a long day of work, school, or travel.
Inaantok means sleepy. The root word is 'antok', meaning sleepiness or drowsiness.
Sabik means excited or eager. It is often used when someone is eagerly anticipating an upcoming event or trip.
Tahimik means quiet. It can describe a person who does not talk much or a place that is peaceful and free of noise.
Maingay means noisy. Use this when a place or a group of people is loud and generating a lot of sound.
Busog means full, specifically referring to the feeling of having eaten enough food and no longer being hungry.
Kinakabahan means nervous or anxious. It captures the jittery feeling before a big presentation, test, or event.
Maganda ang araw translates literally to 'the day is nice'. It is a pleasant expression used to describe good weather or a wonderful day.

sentences.speaker: ate-crystal
sentences.n: In Tagalog, descriptive sentences often place the adjective first, followed by the pronoun and any time markers like 'ngayon' (today).

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: This simple sentence starts with the adjective 'pagod' (tired) followed by the pronoun 'ako' (I), forming a direct statement.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: The preposition 'sa' is used here to link the adjective 'takot' (afraid) to the object of the fear, which is 'kulog' (thunder).

sentences.t: Sabik na sabik si jetjet sa bakasyon.
sentences.e: Jetjet is very excited for the vacation.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

sentences.e: Lola Joli is nervous about the test.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli

sentences.t: Maingay ang mga bata sa labas.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

themes.name: Health & Body
themes.intro: Head, stomach, fever, cough — Tita Baby here with the sensible stuff. Let's hope you never need these words, but learn them anyway!

items.n: Sakit can refer to both physical pain and illness. Depending on context, it changes from a noun meaning sickness to part of a descriptive state.
Masakit is an adjective formed with the prefix ma- attached to sakit. Use this to describe any body part that is currently aching or painful.
Ulo means head. When combined with sakit, it forms the common expression for a headache.
Tiyan refers to the stomach or abdomen. It is frequently used when describing digestive discomfort or hunger.
Ngipin means tooth. Dental pain is very common to describe using the adjective masakit.
Doktor is a loanword derived from Spanish, commonly used in everyday Tagalog alongside traditional terms.
Nars is an adapted loanword from English, widely used in healthcare settings throughout the Philippines.
Gamot means medicine or remedy. It can refer to pills, syrups, or traditional treatments.
Sakit ng ulo literally translates to sickness of the head, which is the standard way to say headache.
Lagnat means fever. It is often reported to doctors or family members when someone feels warm and weak.
Ubo means cough. It is a common symptom often mentioned alongside a cold or fever.
Sipon refers to a common cold or nasal congestion. It frequently accompanies ubo during seasonal changes.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This sentence uses the possessive pronoun ko at the end to indicate whose head hurts, following the standard predicate-subject word order.

sentences.e: I am going to the doctor.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: The verb pupunta is in the future aspect, indicating an action that is about to happen. The preposition sa marks the destination.

sentences.speaker: ate-crystal
sentences.n: The word may indicates existence or possession, meaning to have something. Here it shows that the speaker currently has a fever.

sentences.t: May ubo at sipon si tito.
sentences.e: Uncle has a cough and a cold.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

themes.name: Work & School
themes.intro: Office, exam, meeting, homework — Ate Crystal juggles school and tennis, so she knows this one by heart. Let's go!

items.n: An office or workplace. Often used interchangeably with the native Tagalog word 'tanggapan', though 'opisina' is extremely common in daily conversation due to Spanish influence.
Refers to a boss, employer, or master. Can be used in both professional work settings and domestic contexts.
An employee or worker. Adapted from Spanish 'empleado'. You will often hear this in corporate and business settings.
A student. Derived from the root word 'aral' (study) with the prefix 'mag-' indicating the doer of the action.
An exam or test. It comes from the root 'subok' (to test or try).
A lesson or subject matter to be learned. It uses the suffix '-in' to indicate the object focus.
A book. Borrowed from the Spanish 'libro', though you may also hear the native term 'aklat' in formal writing.
A pencil. Borrowed from Spanish 'lápiz'.
Paper. A direct borrowing from the Spanish 'papel'.
A computer. This is a phonetic borrowing from English, commonly used in offices and schools.
A project or undertaking. Adapted from Spanish, used frequently in both school and work environments.
A meeting or assembly. A native Tagalog word often preferred in formal discussions over the borrowed 'miting'.

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: The location word 'nasa' precedes the place 'opisina', followed by the pronoun 'ako' (I). Word order is predicate-first, common in Tagalog sentence structures.

sentences.speaker: lumpy
sentences.n: The verb 'nag-aaral' is in the continuous aspect. The marker 'ng' connects the verb to its direct object 'Tagalog'.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: The word 'may' indicates existence or possession (there is / we have). It is followed by the noun 'pulong' and the pronoun 'kami'.

sentences.t: Nawala ang lapis ko sa eskwelahan.
sentences.e: My pencil got lost at school.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

sentences.t: Maganda ang proyekto ng mga empleyado.
sentences.speaker: tito-bong

sentences.e: The student is reading a book.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

sentences.t: Kailangan ko ng papel para sa pagsusulit.
sentences.e: I need paper for the exam.
sentences.speaker: lumpy

sentences.t: Mabait ang amo namin sa opisina.
sentences.e: Our boss at the office is kind.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli

themes.name: Questions
themes.intro: Who, what, when, why — Jetjet asks a hundred questions a day! Now it's your turn to ask.

items.n: Ano means "what" and is used to ask for information about things, objects, or situations.
Sino means "who" and is used exclusively when asking about people and their identities.
Kailan means "when" and is used to inquire about time, schedules, or dates.
Bakit means "why" and prompts for reasons, explanations, or motivations behind an action.
Paano means "how" and is used to ask about methods, processes, or ways of doing something.
Alin means "which" and helps single out one or more specific items from a known group.
Ba is a question particle placed after the first word of a sentence to turn a statement into a yes-or-no question.
This phrase means "What is this?" and is perfect for pointing at nearby objects to learn their names.
This phrase means "Who is he or she?" since Tagalog pronouns are gender-neutral for third person.
A casual shorthand meaning "When are we going?" where the destination is understood from context.
A common response meaning "Why not?" used to show agreement or openness to a suggestion.
An inquiry meaning "How do I get there?" used when asking for directions to a place.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This sentence places the question word "Ano" first, followed by the topic marker "ang" and the noun phrase "pangalan mo" (your name).

sentences.speaker: ate-crystal
sentences.n: The structure puts "Sino" at the beginning to ask for the identity of the person who is your friend.

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: Tagalog often places adjectives like "malungkot" right after the question word, followed by the pronoun "ka".

themes.name: Actions
themes.intro: Eating, running, reading, cooking — Ate Crystal is always moving! Let's learn the doing-words.

items.n: Kumakain means eating. It uses the um- infix to indicate an ongoing action in the present tense.
Umiinom means drinking. The root word is inom, combined with the um- prefix for ongoing action.
Naglalakad means walking. It uses the nag- prefix to show an ongoing action.
Tumatakbo means running. The prefix um- turns the root takbo into an active, ongoing verb.
Nagsasalita means speaking. It comes from the root salita and uses the nag- prefix.
Nakikinig means listening. It uses the prefix naki- to show engagement or listening activity.
Nanonood means watching. The root is panood, shifting to nanonood for the present progressive tense.
Nagbabasa means reading. The root basa is paired with the nag- prefix for present tense verbs.
Sumusulat means writing. It takes the root sulat and adds the um- infix for ongoing action.
Nagluluto means cooking. The root luto takes the nag- prefix and partial reduplication to show it is happening now.
Natutulog means sleeping. It uses the prefix natu- to indicate a continuous state of sleep.
Gumagana means working, often used for machines or systems rather than people.

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: This sentence uses the standard VSO (Verb-Subject-Object) structure in Tagalog. 'Ng' acts as the object marker connecting the verb and the mango.

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: The verb comes first (nagbabasa), followed by the pronoun subject (ako), and then the object marked by 'ng' (libro).

sentences.e: He or she is cooking dinner.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: Here, 'siya' means he or she, as Tagalog pronouns are gender-neutral. The sentence places the cooking verb first.

sentences.t: Umiinom ako ng malamig na tubig.
sentences.speaker: lumpy

sentences.e: You are running on the street.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

sentences.e: We are watching a good movie.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

sentences.e: He or she is writing a letter.
sentences.speaker: ate-crystal

sentences.e: The child is sleeping in the room.
sentences.speaker: lola-joli

themes.name: Useful Phrases
themes.intro: These are the phrases that save you — help, wait, slowly, one more time. Lumpy's got your back!

items.n: Tulong means help or assistance. You can use it alone in an emergency or in the phrase 'Kailangan ko ng tulong' when you need someone's aid.
Sandali means moment, and lang means only. Together, 'sandali lang' means 'just a moment' or 'wait a minute'.
Teka is a casual contraction of 'teka lang' or 'hintay ka' meaning wait. It is very common in everyday spoken Tagalog.
Sige is a versatile word meaning okay, sure, or go ahead. It is often used to grant permission or agree to something.
Pwede means can, possible, or may. It is used to ask for permission or express ability, similar to 'can' or 'may' in English.
Dahan-dahan means slowly or carefully. Repeating the root word 'dahan' creates an adverbial form indicating caution or a slow pace.
Muli means again. It is often used when repeating an action, like asking someone to say something muli.
Tama means correct or right. It is the opposite of mali and is frequently used to affirm someone's answer.
Mali means wrong or incorrect. Use this when correcting a mistake or answering a question falsely.
Handa means ready or prepared. You can use this to ask if someone is ready to go or start an activity.
Tapos means finished or done. It can also be used as a conjunction meaning 'then' or 'afterwards' in conversation.
Siguro means maybe or perhaps. It expresses uncertainty about a situation or statement.

sentences.speaker: lumpy
sentences.n: The sentence begins with the predicate 'kailangan' (need), followed by the pronoun 'ko' (I/my), and then the object linker 'ng' connecting it to 'tulong' (help).

sentences.speaker: jetjet
sentences.n: The auxiliary verb 'pwede' comes first, followed by the question particle 'ba'. The pronoun 'ako' becomes 'akong' with the linker before the verb 'magtanong'.

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: This is a short, casual imperative phrase consisting of the shortened word for wait ('teka') and the limiter 'lang' meaning only.

sentences.e: Slowly please / Just take it easy.
sentences.speaker: tita-baby

sentences.e: Maybe he or she is already finished.
sentences.speaker: jetjet

themes.name: Small Talk
themes.intro: Ayos lang? Anong balita? Small talk is how friendships start in the Philippines — let's chat like locals!

items.n: Anong balita? is a casual way to ask 'What's new?' or 'Any news?' among friends.
Ayos lang literally means 'just fine' and is commonly used as a casual reply to greetings.
Use Salamat sa tulong to express gratitude for assistance. 'Tulong' means help.
Walang problema is a popular loan-influenced phrase meaning 'No problem.'
Kaibigan means friend and ko means my, so this phrase introduces a friend.
Mahal kita is a direct and heartfelt way to say 'I love you' in Tagalog.
Ingat ka means 'Take care.' The word 'ka' refers to you singular.
Kita tayo means 'Let's see each other' or 'See you' for making plans.
Pupunta ako means 'I will go.' It uses the future tense reduplication of punta.
Saan ka galing? asks 'Where did you come from?' or 'Where have you been?'
Sarap means delicious, and pagkain means food. This praises a meal.
Magandang araw is a cheerful greeting meaning 'Nice day' or 'Good day.'

sentences.speaker: tito-bong
sentences.n: This sentence places the adjective phrase 'ayos lang' first, followed by the pronoun 'ako' (I).

sentences.speaker: lola-joli
sentences.n: The word 'rin' (also) is added to the end to mean 'Take care too.'

sentences.speaker: tita-baby
sentences.n: The preposition 'sa' introduces the object of gratitude, ending with the possessive pronoun 'mo' (your).
